extracted.intended_audience: mathematics department faculty, program assessment coordinators, and undergraduate administrators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for assessing undergraduate mathematics majors using portfolios and a capstone seminar/comprehensive project. Covers stated program goals, required portfolio contents, review procedures, and capstone project evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departmental capabilities (Northern Illinois University)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of the track a student major may choose, the Department’s baccalaureate program seeks to develop at least five capabilities in the student.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The five capabilities (as adopted) are: 1. To engage effectively and efficiently in problem solving; 2. To reason rigorously in mathematical arguments; 3. To understand and appreciate connections among different areas of mathematics and with other disciplines; 4. To communicate mathematics clearly in ways appropriate to career goals; 5. To think creatively at a level commensurate with career goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portfolio contents and collection procedure (NIU: items a–e)
rubrics_metrics.description: The assessment portfolio should contain specified student work from across the program to provide information related to the departmental capabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chosen items: a) the student’s final examination from the required lower division linear algebra course (for goals 1 and 2); b) the best two projects from the model building course (technical-report style) (for goals 1, 3, 4); c) two homework assignments (midsemester and late) from advanced calculus (for goals 1, 2, 4, 5); d) the best two homework assignments from two other advanced courses determined by emphasis (for all five goals); e) a 250–300 word typed essay discussing the student’s experience in the major emphasizing connections of mathematics with other disciplines (for goals 3 and 4). Instructors collect items a–d into departmental files; the student is responsible for item e. Graduation clearance is contingent on submitting the essay; otherwise the portfolio itself is used for program evaluation only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portfolio review rating scale and committee process (NIU)
rubrics_metrics.description: A committee of senior faculty examines graduating students' portfolios and rates each capability as seen in the portfolio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each capability is rated in one of three categories—strong, acceptable, and weak. After reviewing all portfolios, the committee identifies strengths and weaknesses across students and may make recommendations for program changes or for monitoring procedures; these are forwarded to the Undergraduate Studies Committee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of checklists describing characteristics of student work
rubrics_metrics.description: For each capability, define checklists of observable characteristics of student work that exemplify that capability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (under Problem Solving): student understands the problem (with minor errors? gross errors?), approach is reasonable or appropriate, approach is successful, varied strategies and decision making is evident, informal or intuitive knowledge is applied. Checklists make evaluation more concrete and consistent across reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement and grading to ensure portfolio completion
rubrics_metrics.description: Portfolios will not be produced or thoughtfully completed unless their submission is required and linked to grading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early informal guidelines failed; making submission of the completed portfolio a requirement for passing the mandatory senior capstone course produced complete portfolios, though initially some were last-minute. Integrate portfolio development in required courses and devote class time to reflective writing about how products reflect specific goals to improve depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longitudinal, program-level portfolio design
rubrics_metrics.description: Portfolios should collect student work from various points in the curriculum to allow tracing of growth over the entire program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect artifacts from lower-division, junior- and senior-level courses and include reflective writing. Evaluating portfolios after students graduate helps ensure assessment focuses on program-level outcomes rather than individual students, faculty, or courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplement portfolios with objective instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use objective tests in addition to qualitative portfolio review to provide balanced, program-level assessment data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples used: a test to measure ability in formal operations and abstract logical thought, and a test to determine the stage of intellectual development; plan to administer at freshman and capstone stages. Consider standardized content exams that closely match the curriculum but use them as complementary tools rather than replacing qualitative assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departmental goals for a mathematics major (Saint Mary’s College)
rubrics_metrics.description: Articulation of student achievement goals used to frame assessment around the senior capstone and comprehensive project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The goals listed are: 1. develop learning skills and foundation of fundamental mathematical concepts sufficient for further work or careers; 2. apply mathematical skills and appropriate technology to develop models for problem solving and analysis; 3. communicate ideas and results clearly and precisely, orally and in writing; 4. undertake independent learning beyond formal study; 5. use critical thinking and mathematics as a contributing member of problem-solving teams; 6. have examined and formed ethical principles to guide professional decisions. Use these goals to design capstone tasks and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capstone seminar structure and assessment components (Saint Mary’s)
rubrics_metrics.description: A two-semester Senior Seminar provides both development and assessment via team presentations, independent study, and critiques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fall semester: common text/topic, student teams present and assign/correct problems, students critique presentations, each student must have an advisor and project topic by mid-October; grade based on demonstrated knowledge, presentations, participation, and required paper. Spring semester: preliminary talks, continued advisor meetings, participation and presentation assessed; seminar talks should prepare classmates for the formal presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive project requirements and examination format (Saint Mary’s)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comprehensive project must develop material new to the student and culminates in written and oral examinations before a faculty committee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advisor and student agree on a project of sufficient depth and breadth feasible within the time. Progress is monitored by advisor and seminar director. The final paper is read by a three-member committee (advisor, seminar director, one other). Formal presentation: a forty-minute talk followed by twenty minutes of questions from the faculty committee; the paper and oral performance together constitute the comprehensive examination. Reworking of the paper is common but usually not an impediment to passing. The final paper may serve as an advanced writing portfolio submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive project grading criteria (Saint Mary’s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty discussion and grading of comprehensive projects are based on stated evaluative dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Five explicit criteria used in post-presentation faculty discussion: (1) mastery of the subject, (2) quality of the written paper, (3) quality of the oral presentation, (4) response to questions, (5) independence and reliability shown in the work with the advisor. These criteria are used to determine pass/fail and award honors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit requirements, deadlines, and clear grading criteria are essential
rubrics_metrics.description: For long-term projects and capstone experiences, make all requirements, deadlines, formats, and grading criteria explicit from the beginning to prevent last-minute failures and misunderstanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without deadlines and clear grading expectations weaker students may fall irretrievably behind. Use student critique forms, consider self-evaluation, and be explicit about paper formats and timelines. Faculty must coordinate to resolve differences in interpretation before they become critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative logistics and faculty involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful assessment programs require administrative support for material collection and significant faculty time and engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect most portfolio items through instructors and store in departmental files; Director of Undergraduate Studies must ensure faculty know what to gather and collect essays. Faculty should be willing to serve on committees, monitor deadlines, and provide critiques. Compensate faculty time for portfolio evaluation where possible; if resources are limited, consider sampling portfolios or rotating objectives by year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portfolios are useful even if incomplete but require reading time
rubrics_metrics.description: Incomplete portfolios can still reveal patterns of student performance, but reviewing full folders for each student is time-consuming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portfolios enable tracing student growth and involve many faculty in thinking about the program overall. Expect to allocate substantial faculty time to reading and evaluation; plan for compensation or reduced scope if necessary.
